title: Losing a region without losing the service
description: Redundancy only buys nines when failures are independent. Two regions with separate power, network and deploy pipelines are independent; two racks sharing a switch are not.

nodes.label: Independence is the assumption
nodes.sublabel:
Two replicas sharing a rack,
a power supply, or a deploy
pipeline are not independent —
and the arithmetic that buys
nines no longer applies.

steps.text: GeoDNS returns the address of the region nearest the user. This is genuinely global load balancing — it happens before any packet reaches your infrastructure, which is why it is the only layer that can steer traffic away from a region that is entirely down.
Traffic splits between regions by proximity, and each region serves reads from its own local database. That locality is the point: the cross-continent round trip never lands on the request path.

Data replicates between regions asynchronously. This is where multi-region gets genuinely hard: synchronous cross-region writes cost 100+ ms every time, and asynchronous ones mean the regions disagree.
Health checks stop passing for Region 2 and DNS withdraws its records. The dashed line is a route no longer offered, not a failing request.

All traffic lands on Region 1 — which must have been provisioned to carry it. Two regions each running at 80% capacity cannot absorb each other; that is the hidden cost of active-active and the reason failover capacity is a budget line.
Users near Region 2 are now served from further away, so latency rises. Degraded and available beats fast and down.

The caveat worth stating: DNS TTLs are advisory. Resolvers and client libraries cache addresses beyond them, so some clients keep trying the dead region. DNS is not a fast-failover mechanism — pair it with health-checked load balancers for anything that must move in seconds.
